ABSTRACT Drawing on 1,178 AI risk and reliability papers from 9,439 generative AI papers (January
2020 through March 2025), we compare research outputs from the most influential research institutions:
frontier AI companies (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI) and leading AI
universities (CMU, MIT, NYU, Stanford, UC Berkeley, and University of Washington). We find that
Frontier Corporate AI research increasingly concentrates on pre-deployment areas — model alignment
and testing & evaluation — while attention to deployment-stage issues, such as model bias, has waned
as commercial imperatives and existential risk concerns have taken precedence. We identify significant
research gaps in high-risk deployment domains, including healthcare applications, commercial and financial
contexts, misinformation, persuasive and addictive features, hallucinations, and copyright usage in training
and inference. Without concerted efforts to enhance external observability into AI’s deployment, the growing
concentration of AI research with frontier corporations could deepen knowledge deficits in these critical
deployment areas. We recommend measures to expand external researcher access to deployment data and
improve systematic observability of AI systems’ in-market behaviors.
INDEX TERMS AI governance, AI safety, reliability, generative AI, deployment, policy.
I. INTRODUCTION
As generative AI becomes integrated into every facet of
our work and social lives, risks are emerging in everyday
commercial ‘‘post-deployment’’ contexts [1], [2]. Torts and
litigation are rising, teens have committed suicide, and
hallucinations are causing reliability problems [3]. But we
have little hard data on who or what is responsible for these
effects.
This observability gap, we show, is due to what frontier cor-
porate AI safety & reliability research chooses to focus on and
expose. A handful of frontier AI corporations increasingly
defines the agenda for public AI risk investigations [4] and
focuses on model alignment and testing in pre-deployment
laboratory settings [5] – Figure 4.1 User, system, and society-
level impacts remain neglected.

A. MOTIVATION
The research presented in this paper is motivated by three
observations:
(1) There is a growing disconnect between the theoretical
research being prioritized at the major corporate AI labs,
which examines AI models in isolation, and the growing
need for research on how AI systems function in real-
world deployment contexts where their outputs vary
greatly by prompt, context, and implementation [18],
[19], [20].
(2) Commercial activity is itself a major source of risk
in post-deployment AI systems, yet those in the best
position to monitor and understand those risks have
economic and reputational incentives to underplay them,
rather than conduct transparent research on emerging
problems.
(3) More and more agenda-setting AI research comes from
a small group of incredibly well-resourced corporations,
with enormous relative R&D spending [21] and large
concentrations of Ph.D. graduates [6]. This itself reflects
a compute divide [22] and means collaborations with
AI labs become increasingly important for universities
looking to access frontier models and significant com-
pute [22]. Most public researchers have limited access
to the data needed to assess risks during real-world
deployment.
These observations align with broader patterns docu-
mented in science and technology studies: when research
capacity concentrates in commercial entities, the questions
asked – and not asked – increasingly reflect private rather than
public interests [23]. The ‘‘AI safety’’ agenda itself has been
shaped by particular philosophical and institutional tradi-
tions [24], with implications for which risks receive sustained
attention. Our empirical mapping provides evidence on this
dynamic for generative AI.
Without observability and research on AI systems’
behavior and risks ‘in the wild’, we are flying blind.
Research into model safety that only examines behavior
under controlled laboratory conditions is fundamentally
insufficient, as AI models’ risks and safeguards in practice
often differ significantly from those in theory [25], [26].
Deployment environments dramatically alter model behavior
through varied prompting contexts, fine-tuned applications,
API access patterns, and infrastructure differences [18], [27].
Moreover, AI systems may be used in fundamentally different
ways compared to during testing. Critical post-deployment
components affecting safety include orchestration primitives,
data-retrieval layers such as RAG, safety and guardrail
services, and observability stacks [28].
A structural misalignment between corporate profit incen-
tives and rigorous safety research exacerbates the deployment
research gap. Emerging legal cases highlight this pattern:
real-world harms emerge from deployed systems, compa-
nies respond with minimal changes or counterproductive
measures, and research focus remains predominantly theo-
retical [3], [29]. Character.AI faces lawsuits over addictive
bots encouraging self-harm among teenagers, yet Meta subse-
quently expanded permissions for explicit romantic role-play
with AI bots. OpenAI removed impersonation restrictions for
Sora, enabling deepfakes [30], while nearly 30 lawsuits target
AI developers over copyright infringement [31].
Existing risk disclosures by frontier AI labs focus almost
exclusively on malicious use while ignoring commercial
uses that may cause equivalent harm [32], [33], [34].
Anthropic exemplifies this misalignment: while announcing
interpretability work to find risks in ‘‘model’s inner work-
ings’’ [35], they simultaneously documented actual malicious

B. METHOD
We analyze generative AI risk and reliability research by
leading U.S. institutions using a dataset of 1,178 papers
from 9,439 generative AI papers written by five frontier AI
companies (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft,
and OpenAI), and six leading AI research universities
(Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), MIT, New York
University (NYU), Stanford, UC Berkeley, and University
of Washington) between January 2020 and March 2025.
We call these two groups ‘Corporate AI’ and ‘Academic AI’,
respectively, for short, but really they sample the ‘bleeding
edge’ of AI research – highly influential papers that help set
the AI governance agenda for governments, society, and other
institutions [36], [37].
Our generative AI research dataset is based on OpenAlex,
to which we add research papers from Anthropic and
OpenAI’s websites [38]. We define leading AI risk research
as technical and applied safety and reliability research
pre- and post-deployment. In conjunction with OpenAI’s
o3-mini, we determine if papers are ‘‘safety & reliability’’
research, and then classify them into one of eight sub-
categories. We separately look at generative AI research
into high-risk domains (based on paper abstracts and
titles), covering medical, finance, commercial, & copyright,
misinformation, disclosures, behavioral, & accuracy. Our
sample is intentionally limited to U.S.-based institutions
that set the agenda for frontier AI development; findings
characterize these actors’ research portfolios and should
not be generalized to the broader global AI research
ecosystem.

C. CORE FINDINGS
(1) Among leading AI research institutions in generative AI
risks, frontier corporate research is far more influential.
Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind each have
significantly more citations for their AI safety &
reliability work than any of the major U.S. academic
institutions we track. Google DeepMind has more
citations for its general generative AI research than the
top four AI academic institutions combined.
(2) As frontier AI companies race to commercialize power-
ful AI systems, their research priorities are increasingly
shaped by business incentives rather than by thorough
risk assessments. Most of the governance research by
frontier corporate labs focuses on model performance
divorced from its applications. For example, ethics &
bias research now only receives attention from leading
academic institutions.
(3) Frontier AI companies severely neglect deployment-
stage behavioral and business risks. Only 4% of frontier
corporate AI papers (6% leading Academic AI) tackle
high-stakes areas like persuasion, misinformation, med-
ical & financial contexts, disclosures, or core business
liabilities (IP violations, coding errors, hallucinations) –
despite emerging lawsuits showing these risks to already
be material.
D. POLICY CONSIDERATIONS
Structured access is needed into deployed AI systems’
telemetry data and artifacts in order for third parties to sys-
tematically analyze real-world risks and harms. Monitoring
and evaluation of LLMs in real-world environments is now
essential to quality assurance (QA), as in ‘LLMOps’ [28]. But
the data used for this is the preserve of corporate practice,
resulting in society losing visibility into AI’s ongoing risks
and harms. Academic-industry collaborations are therefore
important but don’t take place on equitable terms [39].
Privacy-preserved external access to data for approved
researchers is a more open, accessible option [40]. This could
draw on companies’ existing telemetry data (logs, traces,
& business metrics) and LLM model data artifacts (e.g.,
training/fine-tuning datasets). Emerging LLM monitoring
frameworks – such as those from LangSmith, Langfuse,
OpenTelemetry, & Weights and Biases – make structured &
standardized external API access for researchers increasingly
feasible. This, however, may expose corporations to liability,
such that safe harbors [41], [42] may be needed to support
purpose-built external access.
E. LITERATURE AND CONTRIBUTION
This study contributes to three literatures. First, within biblio-
metrics of AI research, we extend work mapping institutional
concentration [4], [43] by introducing a pre-/post-deployment
distinction and showing how safety research portfolios differ
across frontier labs and universities. Second, in science
and technology studies (STS), our findings speak to debates
on epistemic capture – the tendency for commercially
embedded research agendas to crowd out public-interest
inquiry [23], [44]; and on how funding structures shape which
questions get asked. Third, we contribute to the emerging
AI governance literature by providing systematic evidence
that deployment-stage risks remain under-researched even at
agenda-setting institutions [10], [38], [45], [46]. Section II
describes our data and method; Section III presents our
key findings; Section IV discusses policy implications; and
Section V concludes. Appendix contains further information
on our sample.

This section describes and justifies the construction of our
dataset of 1,178 AI safety and reliability governance papers
from a total of 9,439 generative AI papers published between
January 2020 and March 2025. Our empirical analysis maps
how safety and reliability work on generative AI is distributed
across a small set of institutions that are central to the
recent ‘‘frontier model’’ wave. We focus on generative AI
and on institutions that (i) design and operate the most
widely deployed large language models and APIs, and (ii)
anchor much of the contemporary machine learning research
ecosystem.
On the corporate side, we include Anthropic, Google
DeepMind (including Google research tagged as DeepMind),
Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI. These five labs collectively
develop and operate the GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama
families, run major commercial APIs, and are focal points in
policy and regulatory debates about AI safety. On the aca-
demic side, we include Carnegie Mellon University (CMU),
MIT, New York University (NYU), Stanford, UC Berkeley,
and University of Washington. These six are chosen because
five of them (excluding NYU) have the highest research
productivity in generative AI safety and reliability research
in OpenAlex.3 To this group we add NYU, which acts as a
rough comparator to Meta given Yann LeCun’s presence at
both institutions.
Our aim is not to describe the entire field, but to ask
whether the institutions with the greatest technical capacity
and closest access to deployed systems appear to prioritize
the kinds of risks that arise once those systems are in real-
world use.
This is a purposeful, critical-case sample, not a represen-
tative sample of all AI research. Our comparisons between
‘‘Corporate AI’’ and ‘‘Academic AI’’ should be interpreted
as contrasts between frontier labs and leading academic
departments, not as estimates for the entire universe of AI-
related work. We use this core set to see how the most
influential actors allocate their safety and reliability research
efforts.

A. CORPUS CONSTRUCTION
We build our corpus from the OpenAlex database,5 queried
via the openalexR package. First, we pull all works with
at least one author affiliated with the ROR IDs corresponding
to our eleven target institutions, published between January
2020 and March 2025. Second, from this institutional pool
we retain only works whose title or abstract indicates a focus
on generative or foundation models.6
This yields our base corpus of 9,439 generative-AI papers
(Table 1). We restrict to standard research outputs (journal
articles, conference papers, preprints, book chapters) and
deduplicate title-level duplicates (e.g., arXiv + conference
versions), keeping the peer-reviewed version where possible.
Because OpenAlex incompletely covers research notes and
reports hosted only on company websites, we supplement the
corporate side by scraping publication lists from Anthropic
and OpenAI, and merging them with the Anthropic and
OpenAI CSVs from Delaney, Guest, and Williams [38],
excluding their DeepMind scrape to avoid double counting.7
These records are reconciled by title/DOI and appended
where OpenAlex coverage is missing. For entries without
abstracts or citation counts in OpenAlex, we retrieve missing
data using publisher APIs (Crossref, Springer, Elsevier) and,
where necessary, HTML scraping. Citation counts are filled
using Google Scholar via SerpApi with fuzzy matching on
titles. The final dataset has abstracts for the vast majority
of works (92 missing) and citation counts missing for only
43 papers.
B. AUTHORSHIP WEIGHTING
Many ML papers have dozens of authors spanning mul-
tiple institutions. To avoid overstating the contributions
of institutions that co-author widely, we use a fractional
authorship approach. For each paper, we identify all authors
and their affiliations. Each author is assigned a single primary
institution: if any affiliation matches one of our eleven target
institutions we use that; otherwise we take the first affiliation

C. IDENTIFYING SAFETY AND RELIABILITY PAPERS
Within this generative-AI corpus we identify the subset of
papers primarily about AI safety and reliability. We define
this as research that: (i) identifies or measures harms, failure
modes, or risks of AI systems, and/or (ii) develops technical,
procedural, or policy measures to make systems safer or more
reliable across the model and product lifecycle (pre- and post-

D. PRE-DEPLOYMENT VERSUS DEPLOYMENT-STAGE
CLASSIFICATION
Several risk categories – notably bias, robustness, and
hallucinations – can manifest at either stage [47]. We classify
papers based on their primary research context:
• Pre-deployment research examines model behavior in
controlled settings prior to public release: laboratory
benchmarks, red-teaming exercises, held-out test sets, and
synthetic adversarial inputs [12], [41]. The goal is to predict
or prevent failures before users encounter them.
• Deployment-stage research studies model behavior in
live systems: real user interactions, production telemetry,
incident reports, and observed harms in specific application
contexts (healthcare, finance, etc.) [28], [48].

(1) Keyword pre-screen. We first flag candidate safety &
reliability papers using a broad keyword filter on titles
and abstracts, covering terms such as safety, risk, robust-

fairness, explainability, interpretability, transparency,
governance, privacy, ethics, responsibility, accountabil-

(2) LLM-assisted inclusion/exclusion. For this candidate set,

automated coder. The model is given the title, abstract,
and our operational definition above, and asked a

incidental/background. The model returns a yes/no label
and a brief justification. We retain only papers labeled
as primarily safety & reliability, yielding 1,178 papers.

E. TOPICAL CLUSTERS AND HIGH-RISK DOMAINS
To analyze where safety & reliability AI governance research
is being directed, we assign each of the 1,178 papers to
one of eight topical clusters: Testing and Evaluation; Align-
ment (Pre-Deployment); Post-Deployment Risks and Model
Traits; Ethics and Bias; Multi-Agent and Agentic Safety;
Interpretability and Transparency; Policy and Governance;
and Privacy and Security.
The clusters are theory-driven and draw on existing tax-
onomies of AI risk and lifecycle evaluation (full definitions
in Appendix C). They are also driven by empirical results: we
want the observed clustering to not all be in a single category.
Using OpenAI’s o3-mini, we provide the title, abstract,
and cluster definitions, and instruct the model to choose the
single best-fitting cluster and justify its choice. Each paper
is thus assigned a single primary topic, which makes the
institutional portfolios easier to compare at a coarse level.
We manually reviewed a sample of classifications across
institutions. Where model labels conflicted with human
judgment or exposed ambiguities in cluster definitions,
we refined prompts and overrode the model’s label. The
most common source of disagreement involved papers
spanning alignment and post-deployment risks – precisely the
boundary we clarify above – resolved by examining whether
empirical evidence came from benchmarks (alignment) or
live systems (post-deployment).
Separately, we tag safety & reliability papers that speak
directly to high-stakes deployment contexts and risk domains
using conservative keyword searches on titles and abstracts.
The categories correspond to those in Table 3: medical,
finance, commercial, misinformation, behavioral risks (e.g.,
persuasion, reward-hacking, sycophancy, addiction), disclo-
sure and auditing, copyright & IP, and accuracy & reliability.
Papers can receive multiple tags (for example, a paper on
hallucinations in medical diagnosis counts as both ‘‘medical’’
and ‘‘accuracy’’). The keyword lists were iteratively refined
to minimize false positives and capture clear, substantive
engagement with each risk area.
We focus on healthcare and finance for three reasons.
First, these are regulatory high-risk categories: the EU
AI Act designates medical devices and creditworthiness
assessments as high-risk applications requiring conformity
assessments [50]; U.S. sectoral regulators (FDA, SEC,
banking agencies) are actively developing AI-specific guid-
ance. Second, these domains involve consequential decisions
affecting health outcomes and economic opportunity, where
errors carry asymmetric costs [51], [52]. Third, they represent
active deployment contexts: frontier models are already
integrated into clinical decision support, diagnostic imaging,
and financial advisory products, creating immediate research
needs. We also include misinformation, behavioral risks, and
copyright – areas where litigation and regulatory scrutiny
are mounting – to capture the breadth of deployment-stage
concerns.
F. LIMITATIONS
Our design has several limitations. First, by construction our
institutional sample covers only U.S.-based frontier labs and
elite research universities. This is a purposive, critical-case
design: we examine institutions that disproportionately shape
AI governance debates, regulatory frameworks, and technical
standards globally [36], [37]. Our findings characterize the
research portfolios of these agenda-setting actors, not a
census of all AI governance research worldwide. Important

work by European institutions (e.g., Alan Turing Institute,

Second, automated and semi-automated classification
inevitably introduces some mis-labeling. We mitigate this
by using a conservative keyword pre-screen, constraining
the model to a small number of clearly defined clusters,
and manually reviewing ambiguous and sampled cases. Our
substantive results focus on large differences in aggregate
shares (for example, the very small fraction of work explicitly
tied to high-risk deployment contexts), which are unlikely to
be overturned by modest classification noise.
Third, we only observe published and publicly listed work.
Internal evaluations, proprietary audits, and confidential
deployment studies conducted inside firms are outside our
dataset. To the extent that corporate labs conduct more post-
deployment research than they publish, our counts understate
their total activity—but that opacity is itself part of the
governance problem we highlight.
Finally, because our sample is intentionally restricted to
frontier labs and elite AI departments, we do not treat the fact
that these entities account for a large share of total citations
as a discovery about the entire AI ecosystem; we use it as
context. Our substantive findings concern the distribution
of effort within their portfolios – for example, the relative
emphasis on pre-deployment testing and alignment versus
post-deployment risks—and the contrast between corporate
and academic actors inside this core set.

1) DISCUSSION OF CAUSES
Early OpenAI work did address post-deployment eval-
uations [87], [88], [89]. But this focus shifted toward
existential risk research and commercial AI applications,
exemplified by their image generator now allowing creation
of brands and real people [25]. The shift stems from
both commercial motivations and ideological influences.
In terms of the latter, corporate alignment research and
evaluations work share origins in existential risk philoso-
phy [90], [91], [92], which emphasizes low-probability but
potentially catastrophic future scenarios. This can be seen
as prioritizing speculative future dangers over immediate
post-deployment concerns and has shaped corporate risk
frameworks – and appears now in emerging research on AI
model ‘values’ and consciousness [65], [93]. This philosophy
permeated Corporate AI research [94] and academia, through
centers like Berkeley’s Center for Human-Compatible
AI (CHAI) and Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered
AI (HAI).
IV. POLICY DISCUSSION
The preceding sections presented our empirical findings:
that frontier corporate labs dominate AI safety research by
citation impact; that their portfolios concentrate on pre-
deployment alignment and evaluation; and that deployment-
stage contexts and high-risk domains remain severely
under-researched. What follows is normative: we argue that
these patterns constitute a governance problem and outline
potential policy responses. Readers may accept our empirical
characterization while disagreeing with the interventions we
propose.
The commercial rollout of large-scale AI systems has
created an information asymmetry that makes rigorous,
public-interest oversight almost impossible. Firms now oper-
ate powerful models behind proprietary interfaces, collecting
exhaustive telemetry – everything from prompts and error
traces to user-level engagement metrics – but that data
seldom leaves the corporate dashboard. Independent scholars
must rely on studying ‘‘incidents’’ after they spill into
the press [95], [96], [97], [98], mining limited chat logs,
[99], [100], [101], and engaging in adversarial and ‘red
teaming’ testing of closed models. Real-world visibility into
the effects of AI systems is negligible. So while companies
have extensive instrumentation, external researchers work
with fragmentary glimpses.
This opacity is not accidental: it is an economically
rational response to litigation risk and competitive pressure.
Detailed corporate logs can indicate bias, privacy leakage,
or manipulative behavior — liabilities no firm wants to
advertise. Yet these same traces – detailed records of system
operations, inputs, outputs, and decision paths – are precisely

One potential pathway is to treat AI telemetry like
financial-market trade data, using a tiered disclosure
regime [102], [103]. For high-risk applications, firms
would expose a secure API that streams three privacy-
protected data feeds: differentially private event logs,
system-operation traces, and model artifact manifests that
record key metadata such as version numbers, training
methods, and documented limitations. Together, this could
allow external researchers to link behaviors observed in
traces to the specific model characteristics that produced
them.
Next, verified academics could access capped samples,
while accredited auditors could obtain deeper access under
NDAs, and regulators would retain subpoena-level rights.
Liability safe harbors would be needed to incentivize
participation from firms and from researchers [41], [42].
Technically, the pieces to make this approach feasible
already exist. Privacy-preserving data access tools have been
used in real-world settings by OpenMined, including for
testing closed-weight LLMs [40]; while LLM telemetry
standards and tools are now being driven by OpenTelemetry
– and use standard JSON trace formats that can be versioned
and rate-limited.
V. CONCLUSION
This paper analyzed 1,178 safety and reliability papers from
9,439 generative AI research publications (2020 through
March 2025) by leading U.S. institutions. We detail a
worrying trend: as deployment of commercial AI mod-
els accelerates, frontier research increasingly concentrates
on pre-deployment areas while high-risk post-deployment
research remains significantly underrepresented.
AI research is highly concentrated within a small number
of frontier companies wielding disproportionate influence
relative to the leading academic institutions in the U.S.
Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and OpenAI’s research
has an outsized impact (measured by citations). Their
research prioritizes technical model alignment and evaluation
approaches that improve product performance. But, as we
see, this may prioritize commercial objectives over societal
ones [3].
Most concerning is the lack of attention to deployment-
stage risks. Only 4% of Frontier Corporate AI papers
and citations tackle high-stakes areas such as persuasion,
misinformation, medical and financial contexts, or core
business liabilities — even as lawsuits demonstrate these
risks are already material. Widely deployed mitigations, like
content moderation and telemetry-based monitoring, remain
virtually unresearched.
The irony is that the corporations with most of the granular
data on live AI systems are the least incentivized to study
resulting harms publicly. But without structured access to
deployment telemetry, external researchers cannot build a
base of public evidence.

If current research priorities persist, we anticipate three
trajectories over the next 5–20 years:

The deployment-research gap will likely widen before
regulatory pressure forces correction. Absent structured
external access, firms will continue to prioritize pre-
deployment capability benchmarking while deployment-

surveillance data that the current research ecosystem is poorly
positioned to supply [47], [104].

deployment-stage research, poorly understood behavioral
dynamics, including persuasion, sycophancy, and depen-

daily life [71], [105]. A mature observability infrastructure,

academic: it determines whether AI integration proceeds with
or without meaningful public oversight.
Other regulated industries with substantial public safety
implications have established independent testing regimes
and mandatory disclosure requirements that as of now have
no equivalent in AI development [106], [107]. Bridging
this gap requires not just incident tracking, but continuous,
structured observability of AI in the wild for governance
through tiered public research, governance, and audit access.

deployment evidence – logs, traces, and metrics – should
become the norm for high-impact AI deployments. Existing
observability stacks already capture these data internally,
and extending them to accredited researchers would impose
minimal overhead while dramatically expanding the public
risk-assessment toolkit. Safe-harbor provisions and tiered-
access APIs can balance liability concerns with transparency.

Berkeley (UC Berkeley), and University of Washington) and

We retrieve from OpenAlex papers published from January

‘‘BERT’’ OR ‘‘transformer’’ OR ‘‘generative model*’’ OR

lexical variations (e.g., ‘‘models’’, ‘‘LLMs’’).
1) DEDUPLICATION AND FILTERING OF PUBLICATION TYPES
We restricted the dataset to standard research outputs (e.g.,
articles, book chapters, preprints) by filtering out items like
editorials, retractions, errata, letters, and purely supplemen-
tary materials. We also ensured that titles appearing multiple
times in different forms (e.g., both a preprint and a published
version) were deduplicated, generally favoring the peer-
reviewed publication type over alternatives.

Because OpenAI and Anthropic publications can sometimes
be sparse in OpenAlex, we merged in additional CSV
files containing each company’s publication data that we
scraped from their websites, combined with the scrape
from Delaney, Guest, and Williams [38] – but excluding
their DeepMind scrape. After ensuring consistent columns,
we appended these records, matched them to ROR IDs for
correct attribution, and again removed duplicates at the title
level.16

For entries missing a DOI, we use the OpenAlex API
using the publication’s OpenAlex ID to retrieve the DOI.
Once DOIs are obtained, we employ multiple strategies to

published by specific organizations like Springer Nature,
Elsevier, or Nature Portfolio, we use their respective APIs
or webpage scraping methods tailored to each publisher’s
content structure. For Springer and Elsevier, valid API keys
are used to authenticate requests and fetch metadata. If API
access fails or isn’t available, web scraping via BeautifulSoup
is used as a fallback to extract abstract text directly from
publisher websites.
We assign citation counts using Google Scholar data via
the SerpApi service. Initially, we attempt a direct title-based
search to extract citation data from the first relevant result.

4) FRACTIONAL CONTRIBUTION
For multi-author papers, we computed each institution’s
fractional contribution based on the number of authors
affiliated with that institution versus total authors on the paper
(e.g., if an institution had 2 authors on a 10-author paper,
it received a fraction of 0.20 for that paper). We retained
only the distinct (paper, institution) pairs for our final dataset,
ensuring one affiliation per author.
This approach does not distinguish among first authors,
last authors, or any hierarchical authorship order; every co-
author is given equal weight. In effect, it ensures each author
is credited exactly once to a single institution. By summing
these fractional shares across all authors, we can then
calculate each institution’s share of total authorship for each
paper, summed over all papers.
